item.title: Ghost-chatting and Consumer Transparency
item.lead: A recurring point in the dossier is the information asymmetry between the presumed conversation partner and the actual execution structure.

blocks.text: According to the source, a user may believe that they are communicating directly with a specific creator, while the interaction is conducted by an employee or team. The dossier links this to consumer law principles regarding deception: if an essential characteristic of the service differs from what a reasonable consumer expects, transparency can become a legal issue.

The precise legal assessment depends on what was promised, what the platform terms state, what information was available beforehand, and what type of service is actually being sold. The source thus formulates a research question, not a universal legal conclusion.

From a regulatory perspective, the subject can be examined in three layers: pre-contractual information, communication during the service, and subsequent data processing. This makes it possible to view ghost-chatting not only as an identity act, but as part of the overall consumer experience.

A model for transparency would, according to the logic of the dossier, minimally clarify when communication is carried out by a team, an automated service, or a third party. Additionally, it must be determined what information about the service is essential for the consumer to make an informed choice.
